title: The Debtor Finance Question: Why the Cash Sitting in Your Invoices Can Be Cheaper Than Your Next Loan
excerpt: Most owners reach for a bigger overdraft or a fresh loan when they need growth capital, overlooking the cash already sitting unpaid in their own invoice ledger and what it could fund instead.
content:
When a business needs capital, most owners reach for the same two options first. A bigger overdraft, or a new loan. That instinct is understandable. They are the products a bank will put on the table without being asked, and they are the ones most owners have used before.

Sitting in the same business, often completely untouched, is a second source of capital that rarely gets a look. It doesn't show up as new debt on a credit file, and in most structures it doesn't ask for a fresh personal guarantee against the family home. It is simply the unpaid invoices already sitting in the debtor ledger, representing work already done and goods already delivered, waiting on terms that might run thirty, sixty or ninety days.

The pattern we typically see across owner-led businesses on the East Coast is that debtor finance gets treated as a last resort, something for businesses in trouble, rather than what it actually is for most users: a straightforward way to bring forward cash that is already owed, so growth doesn't have to wait on a customer's payment terms.

Why the Loan Gets Chosen Before the Ledger Gets Looked At

Part of this is familiarity. A term loan or an overdraft extension is a conversation most owners have had before, with a relationship manager they already know, using a process they already understand. Debtor finance, invoice finance, receivables finance, the terminology varies and none of it feels as settled.

Part of it is also a quiet assumption that using the debtor book for finance signals weakness, that a healthy business shouldn't need to borrow against money it is already owed. That assumption doesn't hold up well against how the facility actually works. A business with strong, diversified customers and a clean debtor book is exactly the profile a financier wants to lend against. It isn't a sign of trouble. It is a sign the asset is worth lending on.

What a Debtor Finance Facility Actually Does

A debtor finance facility advances cash against approved invoices as they are raised, rather than making the business wait out the full payment term. The lender takes security over the receivables themselves, assesses the quality and spread of the debtor book, and charges a fee calculated against the invoice value and the time it remains outstanding. When the customer pays, the facility is squared off and the cycle continues on the next invoice.

The security sits against the receivables, not against the director's home in the way a traditional term loan often requires. That distinction matters more than it first appears. A business that has already taken on a personal guarantee for an equipment loan, a vehicle fleet and a working capital facility is often looking at a meaningfully different risk picture to one that funds its growth through the debtor book instead, and it is worth working through that comparison before the next facility gets signed rather than after.

Where It Fits, and Where It Doesn't

Debtor finance suits businesses with a genuine, recurring debtor book: wholesalers, labour hire and recruitment firms, manufacturers, and professional services businesses invoicing on thirty to ninety day terms. The bigger the gap between delivering the work and getting paid for it, the more useful the facility becomes, because that gap is precisely what it is designed to close.

It suits some businesses poorly. A cash-based hospitality or retail business with no debtor book has nothing to finance against. A business with one or two customers carrying most of the revenue presents a concentration risk that most financiers will price accordingly, or decline outright. And a business whose debtor ledger is already messy, aged and poorly chased is going to find any finance conversation harder than it needs to be, which is its own argument for tightening collections before approaching a lender at all.

A Working Capital Unlock review is often the right starting point here, because it maps exactly how much cash is genuinely trapped in debtors, inventory and supplier terms before anyone commits to a specific finance product. Knowing the real number changes the conversation with a financier considerably.

The Real Comparison, Not Just the Headline Rate

The honest comparison between debtor finance and a traditional loan isn't just the percentage fee against the interest rate. It includes the personal guarantee exposure avoided, the speed of access as the debtor book grows, and whether the facility scales automatically with sales or sits fixed regardless of how the business performs. A term loan is a fixed number that doesn't move with revenue. A debtor finance facility grows as the invoice book grows, which makes it a genuinely different tool for a business in a growth phase rather than a steady state.

None of this means debtor finance is always the better answer. For some businesses, the simplicity and lower administrative load of a traditional facility still wins. The point worth sitting with is that most owners never actually run the comparison, because the loan conversation happens first and the debtor book conversation never gets started. Working through which instrument actually fits a business's cash cycle, debtor spread and growth plans is exactly the kind of structured comparison a fractional CFO brings to the table before a facility gets signed, not after the repayments have already started. If growth capital is the next conversation on your list, it is worth having that comparison made properly, and booking a discovery call is a reasonable place to start it.

faqs.q: What is debtor finance and how does it work for a small business?
faqs.a: Debtor finance lets a business draw cash against its outstanding invoices rather than waiting the full payment term to be paid. The lender advances a percentage of the invoice value, takes security over the receivables, and charges a fee based on the invoice amount and how long it stays outstanding. When the customer pays, the facility settles and the cycle continues.

faqs.q: Is debtor finance the same thing as invoice factoring?
faqs.a: They sit in the same family. Invoice factoring is one specific structure within the broader category of debtor or receivables finance, and the terms are often used loosely and interchangeably. The details that matter are whether customers are notified of the arrangement, who manages collections, and how the fee is calculated, which vary between providers and products.

faqs.q: Does debtor finance require a personal guarantee like a business loan does?
faqs.a: Typically not in the same way. The security generally sits against the receivables themselves rather than the director's personal assets, which is one of the main reasons businesses already carrying meaningful personal guarantee exposure look at debtor finance as an alternative growth funding path. Terms vary by lender, so this is worth confirming on any specific facility.

faqs.q: What kinds of Australian SMEs suit debtor finance best?
faqs.a: Businesses with a genuine, recurring debtor book on thirty to ninety day terms tend to suit it best, including wholesalers, manufacturers, labour hire and recruitment firms, and professional services businesses. Cash-based businesses with no debtor ledger, such as most hospitality and retail operations, have nothing to finance against and generally look elsewhere for working capital.

faqs.q: How quickly can a debtor finance facility be arranged before a busy trading period?
faqs.a: Timeframes vary by lender and by how clean the debtor book already is, but it generally takes longer than most owners expect once due diligence on the customer base is factored in. Businesses anticipating a seasonal sales increase, such as the run into Christmas trading, are better served starting the conversation weeks ahead rather than when the cash gap has already appeared.

faqs.q: How does a business decide between debtor finance and a traditional bank loan?
faqs.a: The decision should weigh more than the headline fee or interest rate. It needs to account for personal guarantee exposure, how the facility scales with sales growth, and the administrative load each option carries. A structured capital raise preparation process is the right way to compare instruments properly before committing to one.

faqs.q: Should a business tidy up its debtor ledger before approaching a financier?
faqs.a: Yes. A debtor book that is aged, poorly documented or inconsistently chased makes any finance conversation harder and can affect the terms on offer. Tightening collections and terms first, often through a dedicated Working Capital Unlock review, puts a business in a stronger position before it sits down with a lender.
